summary.text: A 46-year-old man was admitted in December with a 3-day history of high-grade fever, chills and irritative voiding symptoms, and a one-year history of untreated polydipsia, polyuria and xerostomia. He was a former smoker who quit one month before admission.

On admission he had a temperature of 38.1 °C, heart rate 99 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min and blood pressure 137/83 mmHg, with no meningeal signs. Leukocytosis, raised C-reactive protein and procalcitonin, hyperglycemia, acidosis with raised ketones and HbA1c 12.2% were found. Renal ultrasound and CT showed perinephric changes, bilateral renal swelling, mild hydronephrosis and urinary tract wall thickening.
Severe urinary tract infection and new-onset diabetes with diabetic ketoacidosis were diagnosed and treated with piperacillin-tazobactam, insulin, fluids and electrolyte replacement.

On day 2 he developed bilateral hearing loss, gait instability, expressive dysphasia and psychomotor agitation. Pure-tone audiometry confirmed bilateral sensorineural deafness, antibiotics were escalated to meropenem and empiric methylprednisolone was given. On day 3 he developed pronounced neck stiffness and lumbar puncture showed turbid CSF with purulent meningitis.

CSF mNGS on day 4 identified Klebsiella pneumoniae with rmpA and iucA genes, and urine, blood and CSF cultures grew a string test-positive, ESBL-negative, fully susceptible isolate. CT of the chest and abdomen showed no other metastatic foci, and brain MRI on day 13 showed nodular lesions suggestive of septic emboli or metastatic infection.

Meropenem was increased to 2 g every 8 h with mannitol for intracranial hypertension, then therapy was de-escalated to ceftazidime on day 26. Fever and meningeal signs resolved but the bilateral deafness persisted. He was discharged in stable condition after 32 days with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and insulin, and at 8 months had no recurrent infection but permanent deafness and declined further follow-up MRI.
